subject: Copywriting
title: Media Literacy as Self-Defense
description: A quick, practical guide to Media Literacy as Self-Defense.

hook.text: Finland teaches media literacy from age 6. It's ranked the most resistant country to disinformation in Europe.

buildup.text: Media literacy means identifying source, intent, and technique. Who wrote this? Why?

discovery.text: The CRAAP test evaluates information: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose.

twist.text: Media literacy doesn't make you immune—it makes you slower to react.

climax.text: The best defense against propaganda isn't blocking it—it's teaching people to recognize it. Inoculation beats.

punchline.text: Finland teaches media literacy at age 6. Education is the best defense.

quiz.question: What does the CRAAP test evaluate?
options: Content quality through Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose

details.summary: Media literacy is the ability to critically analyze and evaluate media messages — the intellectual self-defense against propaganda. It involves questioning sources, recognizing emotional manipulation, identifying logical fallacies, and understanding who benefits from any given message.
details.whyItMatters: In an era of information warfare, media literacy is as fundamental as reading literacy. It transforms passive consumers of information into active, critical thinkers who are harder to manipulate.
takeaways: Media literacy means asking who created a message, why, and for whom
Emotional awareness helps identify when feelings are being deliberately triggered
Source evaluation is the foundation of critical media consumption

faq.question: What are the key questions of media literacy?
faq.answer: Who created this message? What techniques are being used to attract my attention? What values or points of view are included or omitted? Why was this message sent? Who profits from this message? These five questions form the foundation of critical media analysis.

faq.question: Can media literacy be taught to children?
faq.answer: Yes, and experts argue it should be a core subject alongside reading and math. Finland leads the world in media literacy education, integrating it across all subjects from kindergarten, and its citizens consistently score highest on resistance to misinformation.
